overlays.question: Oxygen pulls shared electrons closer. Which atom becomes δ−?

options.label: Oxygen
options.feedback: Right — oxygen pulls electrons toward itself, so it carries the partial negative charge.

options.label: Hydrogen
options.feedback: H loses electron density to oxygen, so H goes δ+. The stronger puller gets δ−.

overlays.rule: Higher electronegativity wins the electrons — and gets the δ−.
overlays.hint: Which atom is more electronegative — 3.5 or 2.1?

overlays.question: What kind of bond holds two water molecules side-by-side?

options.label: Hydrogen bond
options.feedback: Yes — δ+ H of one water attracts δ− O of another. Weak but everywhere.

options.label: Covalent bond
options.feedback: Covalent is INSIDE one water molecule (O–H). Between molecules is hydrogen bonding.

options.label: Ionic bond
options.feedback: No ions in pure water. Just partial charges attracting each other.

overlays.rule: Covalent = INSIDE one molecule. H-bond = BETWEEN molecules.
overlays.hint: Are full charges involved here, or just partial ones?

overlays.question: pH drops from 6 to 5. H⁺ concentration changed by how much?

options.label: 1× — small step
options.feedback: pH is logarithmic, not linear. 1 unit = 10× change. AP loves this trap.

options.label: 10× more H⁺
options.feedback: Right — each pH unit is a factor of 10. Small number, huge effect.

options.label: 100× more H⁺
options.feedback: Each unit is 10×. Two units would be 100×. You only went 1 unit.

overlays.rule: pH is logarithmic — each 1-unit change = 10× change in H⁺.
overlays.hint: pH stands for the negative LOG of [H⁺].

overlays.question: Heat hits an enzyme. Which bonds break first and disable it?

options.label: Hydrogen bonds in tertiary structure
options.feedback: Right — weak H-bonds holding the 3D shape break first. The enzyme unfolds.

options.label: Peptide covalent bonds
options.feedback: Covalent peptide bonds are far too strong for just heat. That's denaturation vs digestion.

overlays.rule: Phase transitions break intermolecular networks first — covalent bonds stay intact.
overlays.hint: Weak bonds go first. Which interactions hold the FOLD, not the chain itself?

overlays.question: How many covalent bonds can a single carbon make?

options.feedback: That's water's hydrogen count. Carbon has 4 valence slots — it makes 4 bonds.
Right — 4 bonds. That's why carbon makes long branched chains, the backbone of every organic molecule.
Carbon has 4 valence electrons, not 8 bonds. 4 is the magic number.

overlays.rule: Carbon = 4 bonds. Every organic molecule is built on that fact.
overlays.hint: Think valence electrons in the outer shell.

overlays.question: C₄H₁₀ describes exactly ONE specific molecule. True?

options.label: True — formula = identity
options.feedback: Trap. Butane AND isobutane are both C₄H₁₀. Same formula, different shape, different behavior.

options.label: False — could be isomers
options.feedback: Right — same molecular formula can have multiple structural arrangements. Shape ≠ formula.

overlays.rule: Molecular formula = count. Structural formula = arrangement. AP tests arrangement.
overlays.hint: What if you branch the chain in the middle?

overlays.question: An amino acid's carboxyl (–COOH) group — what does it do with H⁺?

options.label: Donates H⁺ (acid)
options.feedback: Right — carboxyl gives up its H⁺ easily. That's why it's classified as an acidic group.

options.label: Accepts H⁺ (base)
options.feedback: That's amino (–NH₂). Carboxyl donates. The –OH end loses its H⁺.

overlays.rule: Carboxyl = donates H⁺ (acid). Amino = accepts H⁺ (base).
overlays.hint: The word 'carboxylic ACID' is a hint.

overlays.question: Hydroxyl (–OH) groups make a molecule fully charged. True?

options.label: Yes — –OH = charge
options.feedback: Trap. –OH makes the molecule POLAR but not charged. δ+/δ− are partial, not full.

options.label: No — polar, not charged
options.feedback: Right — hydroxyl creates partial charges via electronegativity. Polar ≠ ionic.

overlays.rule: Polar (partial charge δ) ≠ charged (full + or −). AP grades this distinction.
overlays.hint: Has any electron been fully transferred, or just shared unequally?

overlays.question: Chain alpha-glucose together. The polymer's shape is:

options.label: Coiled / helical
options.feedback: Right — alpha linkage bends each junction. Many bends = coil. That's why starch packs into granules.

options.label: Straight and rigid
options.feedback: That's beta-glucose → cellulose. Alpha bends, beta stays straight.

overlays.rule: Alpha → coiled (storage). Beta → straight (structure).
overlays.hint: Which version was the one with a slight bend at each link?

overlays.question: Same monomer (glucose), different linkage. Same function?

options.label: Yes — same monomer = same role
options.feedback: Trap. Starch (alpha) is energy storage. Cellulose (beta) is structural. Linkage decides everything.

options.label: No — linkage changes function
options.feedback: Right — one bond flip is the entire reason starch is digestible and cellulose isn't.

overlays.rule: Monomer identity ≠ polymer function. Linkage geometry decides the role.
overlays.hint: Same Lego brick, different snap orientation. Same final tower?

overlays.question: A human eats raw cellulose. What happens to it?

options.label: Digested like starch
options.feedback: We have amylase (alpha-only). No cellulase = no breakdown. It passes through as fiber.

options.label: Passes through as fiber
options.feedback: Right — wrong enzyme shape. Amylase can't bind beta-linkages. Cellulose exits intact.

overlays.rule: Enzyme specificity = shape match. Wrong shape = no reaction, no matter how 'similar' the substrate.
overlays.hint: Which enzyme do you actually make — amylase or cellulase?

overlays.question: Cows digest grass. Why can they when we can't?

options.label: Cows produce cellulase themselves
options.feedback: Cows don't make cellulase either. Their gut BACTERIA do. Symbiosis, not new cow biology.

options.label: Gut bacteria do it for them
options.feedback: Right — cows host cellulase-producing bacteria. Same enzyme-shape logic, just outsourced.

overlays.rule: Same chemistry, outsourced biology. Symbiotic enzyme strategies appear all over AP Bio.
overlays.hint: Cows are not chemically different from humans — but they host different…?

overlays.question: Unsaturated fatty acid has a kink. Membrane fluidity is:

options.label: More fluid
options.feedback: Right — kinks prevent tight packing. Gaps between chains keep the membrane flexible.

options.label: Less fluid
options.feedback: That's saturated (straight, packs tight). Kinks = looser packing = more fluid.

overlays.rule: Kink → can't pack → more fluid. Straight → packs → more rigid.
overlays.hint: Can bent straws pack together as tightly as straight ones?

overlays.question: Cold-water fish — which fatty acid type dominates in their membranes?

options.label: Saturated (straight)
options.feedback: Cold would make saturated membranes too rigid. Fish need MORE fluidity in cold, not less.

options.label: Unsaturated (kinked)
options.feedback: Right — cold stiffens membranes, so fish pre-compensate with kinked tails. Structural logic, not random.

overlays.rule: Membranes adapt: cold → more unsaturated. Warm → more saturated. Compensation principle.
overlays.hint: What would cold do to the membrane WITHOUT this adaptation?

overlays.question: Cholesterol always makes membranes more fluid. True?

options.label: True
options.feedback: Trap. Cholesterol is a BUFFER — increases fluidity in cold, DECREASES it in heat. Context-dependent.

options.label: False — depends on temperature
options.feedback: Right — same molecule, opposite effects depending on temp. That's the buffer mechanism AP tests.

overlays.rule: Cholesterol = fluidity buffer. Effect depends on context — high temp or low temp.
overlays.hint: What word does the script use — 'fluidity ___'?

overlays.question: Membrane is at HIGH temperature. Cholesterol's effect on fluidity?

options.label: Increases fluidity further
options.feedback: Counterintuitive but no. At high temp the membrane is already too loose — cholesterol restricts movement.

options.label: Decreases fluidity
options.feedback: Right — cholesterol's rigid rings restrict over-active tails. Buffer kicks in opposite to need.

overlays.rule: High temp → cholesterol decreases fluidity. Low temp → cholesterol increases fluidity.
overlays.hint: If the membrane is already too loose, what would a stiffener do?

overlays.question: Peptide bonds in primary structure are:

options.label: Hydrogen bonds (weak)
options.feedback: H-bonds hold SECONDARY structure. Peptide bonds are stronger — they survive denaturation.

options.label: Covalent (strong)
options.feedback: Right — peptide = covalent. That's why primary structure survives heat and pH changes.

overlays.rule: Primary = covalent peptide bonds. The only level that survives denaturation.
overlays.hint: Which bonds get broken when something just unfolds, not falls apart?

overlays.question: Secondary structure (alpha helix, beta sheet) is held by — what?

options.label: H-bonds between R-groups
options.feedback: Trap. R-group interactions hold TERTIARY structure. Secondary = backbone H-bonds, not R-groups.

options.label: H-bonds in the backbone
options.feedback: Right — secondary uses backbone carbonyl + amino H-bonds. R-groups don't enter until tertiary.

overlays.rule: Secondary = BACKBONE H-bonds. Tertiary = R-GROUP interactions. Distinguishing these is AP gold.
overlays.hint: Where are the H-bonds in an alpha helix — on side chains or on the chain itself?

overlays.question: An enzyme denatures from heat. Has it been digested?

options.label: Yes — bonds are broken
options.feedback: Denaturation = unfolding. Hydrolysis = chopping into amino acids. Denatured ≠ digested.

options.label: No — just unfolded
options.feedback: Right — denatured proteins are still one polypeptide. Peptide bonds intact. Just lost the shape.

overlays.rule: Denaturation = unfold. Hydrolysis = break peptide bonds. AP penalizes confusing these.
overlays.hint: Are the amino acids still connected, or in pieces?

overlays.question: Heat denatures a protein. Which bonds SURVIVE the unfolding?

options.label: Peptide bonds (covalent)
options.feedback: Right — covalent peptide bonds are too strong for heat. Only H-bonds + ionic + hydrophobic break.

options.label: Hydrogen bonds in helices
options.feedback: Those go first — they hold secondary together. Heat breaks weak interactions, not covalent ones.

overlays.rule: Heat denatures weak bonds (H-bond, ionic, hydrophobic). Strong covalent bonds survive.
overlays.hint: Strong vs weak — which kind does mild heat actually disrupt?
